questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a component takes responsibility for
questions.learningObjective: identify the part of a screen that belongs inside a component
questions.stem: A component takes a list of orders as input and returns the markup for a table of them. Which of these belongs inside that component rather than beside it?

options.text: The state of its own filter box and the rule that turns orders into rows
The route the table is shown on and the address of every row link
options.misconception: believes routing belongs to a component because the component draws the rows

options.text: The data source that fills the orders list and the server that answers it
options.misconception: believes a component owns the transport that produced its data

options.text: The shared colour and spacing values used by this table and by others
options.misconception: believes shared design values must be duplicated inside each component

questions.explanation: A component is the unit that owns rendering and the state that rendering depends on, and it receives everything else from outside. The filter text and the mapping from orders to rows are both local: nobody else needs to know the rule, and if the rule changes only this component has to change. The route, the transport and the design values are all shared, so putting them inside one component would mean every screen keeps its own copy and they can drift apart. The test is simple: if two different screens would need the same answer, it is not this component's private business.
questions.hint: Ask what two different screens would both need to know.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: One-way data flow when a child edits a value
questions.learningObjective: choose the pattern that keeps props flowing one way when a child edits
questions.stem: A child component is handed a title as a prop and must let the user edit that title. Which arrangement keeps the data flowing one way?

options.text: Hold the draft in the child's own state and hand the finished title to a callback
Assign the edited title straight into the props object the parent handed down
options.misconception: believes a child may rewrite the props object it was given

options.text: Keep the edited title in a module variable that both components import and read
options.misconception: believes a shared module variable is a one-way channel between parent and child

options.text: Read the title from the DOM node on every render instead of recording the edit
options.misconception: believes reading the DOM is an acceptable substitute for tracking a change

questions.explanation: One way means the parent decides what the title is and the child reports what happened; the child never becomes the writer of the parent's value. A draft in local state is the child's own business, and calling back is the child asking rather than deciding, which is why the parent can accept, transform, or refuse the change. Writing into the props object mutates something the parent still holds and leaves the two disagreeing with no record of who changed what. A module variable is shared but not one-way: either side can write it, nothing re-renders when it changes, and the flow becomes invisible. Reading the DOM works only until two nodes show the same text.
questions.hint: Ask who is allowed to decide the final value of the title.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Each render reads a fixed snapshot of state
questions.learningObjective: state what a finished render keeps reading after state changes
questions.stem: A render reads the count and copies it into a local variable, and only then does an event handler change the count. What does the render that already finished go on reading?

options.text: The value from the render it was part of, because every render gets its own snapshot
The newest value, because the local variable is a live view of the state itself
options.misconception: believes a value copied during a render keeps tracking the state afterwards

options.text: The newest value, because the framework rewrites every earlier render's variables
options.misconception: believes the framework goes back and updates variables of past renders

options.text: Nothing at all, because the local variable is cleared when the render returns
options.misconception: believes a render's variables do not survive the render that made them

questions.explanation: The whole point of describing a render as reading a snapshot is that the values it read cannot move underneath it. A render is a function call: it opened, it read, and it produced markup, and the variables it declared belong to that call. A later change starts a new render rather than editing the old one, which is what makes reasoning about a component tractable, and it is why reading a value in a handler and using it later can be wrong. The live-view belief is the source of most stale-value reports, because it is natural to assume a name and a value stay welded together after the fact.
questions.hint: Ask whether the framework can edit a call that has already returned.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Batching the writes made in one event
questions.learningObjective: trace the render count and the value seen when one handler writes twice
questions.stem: One click handler runs `setTab('billing'); setTab('summary');`, and both calls belong to the same event. How many render passes does the component make, and what is the value of tab when that render runs?

options.text: One render pass, and it sees summary, because the two writes are batched together
Two render passes, one per write, and the first of them sees billing
options.misconception: believes each write to the same key renders on its own immediately

options.text: One render pass, and it sees billing, because the first write to a key wins
options.misconception: believes the earliest queued write for a key is the one applied

options.text: Two render passes, and the later one sees summary, because writes apply in turn
options.misconception: believes queued writes each produce a render before the next is applied

questions.explanation: Writes requested during one event are collected and applied together before the component is called again, so the two calls to the setter produce a single render pass, not two. Applying the queue means the second write to the same key overwrites the first, so the render sees the value that was written last. The trap is assuming a setter call is a render: a setter is a request, and until the event's work is finished nothing has been rendered at all. That is also why a render can never observe the intermediate value, however plausible it looks in the source.
questions.hint: Ask whether a setter call renders, or only asks for a render.

questions.topic: Two writes built from a value the render captured
questions.learningObjective: trace the final state when both updates read the same captured value
questions.stem: A render does `const count = state.count;` and gets 0. One click handler then runs `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 10);`. What value does count hold after the render that follows the handler?

options.text: 10, because both new values were built from the 0 that render captured
11, because the second write reads the value the first one produced
options.misconception: believes a plain value argument re-reads the state when it is applied

options.text: 1, because a later write to the same key replaces the earlier queued value
options.misconception: believes the earliest write to a key is the one that survives

options.text: 0, because the render's local variable is the value the setter reads back
options.misconception: believes the setter consults the render's variable instead of the state

questions.explanation: Both arguments are ordinary values, and both were computed before either write was applied, so both are 0 plus something: 1 and 10. Applying the queue in order leaves the last one standing, which is 10, and the single render that follows sees 10. Nothing here re-reads the state between the two calls, because the two expressions were already finished before the first setter ran. The belief that the second write sees the first is exactly what a function argument would do, which is why the fix is to pass a function and let the framework supply the previous value.
questions.hint: Ask when the two expressions on the right of the setters were evaluated.

questions.topic: The functional form of a state update
questions.learningObjective: trace the final state when both updates are functions of the previous value
questions.stem: The count is 0 before a click handler begins. The handler runs `setCount(c => c + 1);` and then `setCount(c => c + 10);`. What value does the count hold after the one render that follows?

options.text: 11, because the second function is given the value the first one produced
10, because both functions are given the count from before the handler
options.misconception: believes a function argument also receives the count from the render

options.text: 1, because the first write replaces what the second function was going to see
options.misconception: believes the first write cancels the rest of the queue

options.text: 12, because the framework adds one to the previous value before each call
options.misconception: believes a functional update is applied on top of an automatic increment

questions.explanation: A function passed to the setter is not called at the moment it is written; it is called when the queue is applied, and it is handed the value the key holds at that point. The first call therefore turns 0 into 1, and the second is handed 1 and produces 11, all before the single render. That is the whole reason this form exists: it makes each update a function of the current value rather than of a value read earlier, so a burst of related writes in one handler cannot lose an increment. Passing plain values works only when the new value does not depend on the old one.
questions.hint: Ask when the function is called and what it is handed.

questions.topic: A handler frozen at the render that created it
questions.learningObjective: trace the value a long-lived handler reads from its own render
questions.stem: A component builds a handler `() => report(count)` during a render and registers it once with `useEffect(() => { subscribe(onClick); }, []);`. The count then becomes 1 and then 2, and the handler is never replaced. What does calling it report?

options.text: 0, because the handler still closes over the binding from its first render
1, because the framework rebinds the variable to the value before the change
options.misconception: believes the framework updates a closed-over variable in a past render

options.text: 2, because the handler reads the newest value each time it is called
options.misconception: believes a closure over state always sees the current value

options.text: 0, because an empty dependency list stops the component re-rendering entirely
options.misconception: believes an empty dependency list freezes the component's own rendering

questions.explanation: A handler is an ordinary function value, and the variables it reads are the ones belonging to the render that created it. Since the handler was made during the render where the count was 0, that is the binding it reads, and every call reports 0 no matter how far the state has moved on. Keeping the handler stable is useful, but stability and freshness are different properties: an empty dependency list gives the first one and takes away the second. The same reasoning applies to a value, an array, or anything else captured, and it is why a handler that must read current state has to be given a way to fetch it rather than holding a copy.
questions.hint: Ask which render's variables the function was created alongside.

questions.topic: When a memoised child is actually reused
questions.learningObjective: count the renders of a memoised child given stable and fresh props
questions.stem: A parent passes an array of two items to a memoised child. Three parent renders pass the same array it built once, then two more each build a new array holding the same two items. How many times does the child's function run?

options.text: 3 times, because only the two newly built arrays fail the comparison
1 time, because a memoised child compares contents and both arrays match
options.misconception: believes memoisation compares the contents of an array prop

options.text: 5 times, because a prop that is an array always forces a fresh render
options.misconception: believes any array-valued prop defeats the reuse every time

options.text: 2 times, because the first render is skipped and the shared array is reused
options.misconception: believes the first render of a memoised child is not counted

questions.explanation: Reuse is decided by comparing each prop with the previous render's value for the same prop, using identity rather than contents, so the three renders that hand over the same array produce one child render in total. Each of the two newly built arrays is a different object, so each of those renders runs the child again, for three runs overall. The trap is that the arrays are equal in every element and still not equal as props, which is why a parent that builds an array or an object inline defeats the memoisation on every render no matter how stable the data is.
questions.hint: Ask how the comparison treats two arrays with the same two items in them.

questions.topic: A stored total that outlives the items it came from
questions.learningObjective: trace the value a derived value stored in state reports after the input changes
questions.stem: A cart keeps its total in state beside its items, and the render does `const total = state.total;`. The lines are worth 10 and 12, so the stored total is 22. A later render supplies one line worth 5 and nothing recomputes the total. What does it show?

options.text: 22, because a stored total is state and only a state update can change it
5, because the render recomputes the total from the items on every pass
options.misconception: believes rendering recomputes a total that is already in state

options.text: 17, because the new line is added to the total that was stored before
options.misconception: believes a stored total is adjusted automatically when items change

options.text: 0, because a stored total is discarded when its items are replaced
options.misconception: believes replacing the items clears the total that was computed from them

questions.explanation: Once a total lives in state it is an ordinary fact like any other, and nothing links it to the items any more. The render that supplied the new line read the stored 22 and printed it, and the correct answer for those items, 5, exists only if something computes it. This is the cost of storing a derived value: there are now two places the answer can live, and every future path that changes the items has to remember to change the copy. Keeping the items and computing the total while rendering removes the second place, and the extra arithmetic is usually cheaper than the bug.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything in the render consults the items to produce the total.

questions.topic: Two in-flight requests writing the same state
questions.learningObjective: trace which of two overlapping responses reaches the state last
questions.stem: A screen starts `fetch('/orders/1')`, answered after 300 ms with an older value, then `fetch('/orders/2')`, answered after 100 ms with a newer one. Both handlers assign into the same state. What ends up on screen?

options.text: The value from /orders/1, because the last response to arrive wins the state
The value from /orders/2, because the request that started last is the freshest
options.misconception: believes the most recently started request is the one that should win

options.text: The value from /orders/2, because an answer to a superseded request is dropped
options.misconception: believes the framework discards the answer to a request that has been overtaken

options.text: The value from /orders/1, because every request is awaited before the page updates
options.misconception: believes the framework waits for all requests before committing state

questions.explanation: Whichever response arrives last performs its assignment last, and there is nothing in this code to say otherwise, so the slower first request overwrites the faster second one and the screen shows the older value. The order of the calls in the source says nothing about the order of the answers, because the network is what decides when each one completes. Nothing in the framework is tracking which request is current, so the fix has to be in the code: either cancel the earlier request when a newer one starts, or record which request is wanted and drop any answer that is no longer wanted.
questions.hint: Ask which assignment happens last in time rather than in the source.

questions.topic: Which values are inputs and which are consequences
questions.learningObjective: choose the arrangement that keeps a computed figure correct by itself
questions.stem: A list component holds both the items and the number of items matching the current filter. Which arrangement keeps the count right without any extra work?

options.text: Hold only the items, and work the matching count out while rendering
Hold both, and set the count in a setter whenever the filter text changes
options.misconception: believes matching the filter text is the only change that affects the count

options.text: Hold both, and recompute the count in an effect that watches the filter value
options.misconception: believes an effect watching the filter also reacts to the items changing

options.text: Hold only the count, and rebuild the matching items from it on each render
options.misconception: believes a count carries enough information to recover the items

questions.explanation: The count is a function of the items and the filter text, so it is a consequence and not an independent fact. If only the inputs are stored, the consequence is produced fresh on every render and is wrong only if the logic is wrong. Storing it means every path that changes the items, whether an add, a delete, a reload from the server, or an undo, has to remember to update the count as well, and the path that forgets is the bug. An effect does not solve this either, because it only re-runs for the values it watches, and the items are exactly as capable of changing the count as the filter is.
questions.hint: Ask what the count is a function of, and whether the items can change too.

questions.topic: Where shared state belongs in the tree
questions.learningObjective: place state at the closest common parent of the components that read it
questions.stem: A filter box and the list it filters are two sibling components, both under one parent. Which component should hold the filter text?

options.text: The closest common parent, passing the value down and the change back up
The filter box, writing the text into a shared store the list reads
options.misconception: believes a shared store is a simpler answer than passing a value down

options.text: The list, holding the text and passing it into the filter box as a prop
options.misconception: believes the component that displays a result should own the input

options.text: The router, keeping the text in the address so both components read it
options.misconception: believes every piece of shared state belongs in the address

For two siblings that is their parent: it holds the value, hands it to the box as a prop, receives the change through a callback, and hands it to the list as another prop. Going lower means one of the two cannot see it without a shared store or a lifted value that has escaped the tree, and going higher works but pushes the value through components that never read it. The address is a reasonable place for a value that should survive a reload and be shareable, which is a separate question from where it is most convenient to hold.
questions.hint: Ask for the lowest component that both readers can be reached from.

questions.topic: A controlled input whose handler stores nothing
questions.learningObjective: predict what a controlled field shows when its change is never recorded
questions.stem: A search box is written as `<input value={query} onChange={onQuery} />`, and `onQuery` logs the event without storing the text anywhere. What does the user see as they type?

options.text: The box empties after each key, because the render keeps putting back an empty value
The text appears normally, because the browser keeps whatever was typed
options.misconception: believes the browser's own value survives a render that sets it

options.text: The box fills with the word undefined, because a missing value renders as that
options.misconception: believes an absent value is printed as the text undefined

options.text: The text appears only after a reload, because rendering is postponed until then
options.misconception: believes the field is not re-rendered until the page is reloaded

questions.explanation: A controlled field has no memory of its own: whatever the render supplies as the value is what the field ends up showing, and the framework writes that back after every change event. Since the state behind this value never changes, the value supplied is still empty, so each keystroke is undone and the field never grows past nothing. This is the usual first symptom of a change handler that logs instead of setting state, and it looks like a key-handling fault rather than a data-flow one. An uncontrolled field is the other arrangement: it keeps whatever the user typed and the application reads that value when it needs it.

questions.learningObjective: identify the change that separates data access from rendering
questions.stem: One component calls fetch on mount and returns the table it builds, so the request, the loading flag, the error text and the row markup all live in one function. Which single change separates the two concerns?

options.text: Move the request, the flag and the error text into a hook the component calls
Wrap the fetch call in a try block, so the separate error text is no longer needed
options.misconception: believes a try block removes the need to represent the failed state

options.text: Move the row markup into a second component that takes the items as a prop
options.misconception: believes splitting the markup alone separates fetching from rendering

options.text: Add a dependency list to the effect, so the request only runs on mount
options.misconception: believes limiting how often the request runs separates the two concerns

questions.topic: Why a list needs a key that is not its position
questions.learningObjective: state what a key is for in a rendered list
questions.stem: A list renders four rows with `key={item.id}`, then a fifth row is inserted at the front. Why must the key identify the row rather than its position in the array?

options.text: The key tells the renderer which old row is which new one, so state survives
The key becomes the row's DOM id, so the browser can find that row again
options.misconception: believes the key is written into the document as an identifier

options.text: The key orders the rows, so a new first row is placed at the end instead
options.misconception: believes a key decides where a row appears in the list

options.text: The key caches each row's output, so the four existing rows are never rebuilt
options.misconception: believes a key makes the renderer skip rows that were not changed

With positions as keys, inserting at the front renumbers every row, so the renderer concludes that row one became row two, and the state each row held travels to the wrong piece of data. The key is not an id in the document and it does not order anything, and it does not by itself stop rows from re-rendering; it only says which row is which.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a stored derived value eventually disagrees with its input
questions.learningObjective: explain the cost of storing a value that can be computed instead
questions.stem: Explain why keeping a filtered item count in state next to the list it came from eventually shows a number that does not match the list, and say what should be stored instead.

answer.exemplar: The count is not a fact of its own; it is what the list and the filter text produce at one moment, so storing it creates a second copy of a value that already exists elsewhere. A copy only changes when something remembers to change it, and the things that change the list are not limited to changing the filter: adding a row, deleting one, receiving a fresh copy from the server and undoing an edit all alter what the count should be. Any of those paths that does not also write the count leaves the two disagreeing, and nothing in the render notices because a stored value looks exactly like a correct one. What should be stored is the list and the filter text, because those are the inputs; the count is then produced while rendering and is right whenever the inputs are right. The tempting argument for storing it is that counting on every render is wasted work, but that work is trivial beside the debugging time a stale copy costs, and the caching only pays off once the counting is genuinely expensive.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to name the count as a consequence rather than an independent fact, list the change paths that can move the list without touching the count, and conclude that the inputs are what belong in state. Merely saying that a duplicate is bad misses the mechanism, which is that a copy is only as current as the last time somebody remembered to update it.
questions.hint: Start by asking what the count is a function of, then list the ways the list can change.

questions.topic: The reach of an error boundary
questions.learningObjective: explain what an error boundary catches and what it cannot
questions.stem: Explain which failures an error boundary catches, which it does not, and why the second group needs a different mechanism.

answer.exemplar: A boundary is a component, so the only code it surrounds is the code called while components render: a child that throws while computing its own output, a value that was expected to be an object and is not, a helper called during rendering that throws. Those failures happen inside the render of the subtree, the boundary catches them, and it renders its fallback in place of the failed part while the rest of the page carries on. The failures it cannot catch are the ones that happen outside that call: a click handler that runs long after the render returned, a promise that rejects later, a timer callback, and anything that fails on the server while the page is being produced. Those have no boundary in the call stack when they go wrong, so they reach the page instead. That is why one mechanism is never enough: the boundary covers the part of the code whose failures are synchronous with rendering, and handlers need their own handling, which means a failure has to be turned into something the component can render rather than being allowed to escape. The trap is that the two look identical at the call site, since both are a throw inside the same file, and a boundary that appears to be unreliable is usually being relied on for the wrong one.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to tie the boundary's reach to the fact that it is a component and can only surround rendering, name at least one failure that escapes it, and say what handles that group instead. Saying it catches errors in its subtree is the answer that is already wrong, since the subtree is exactly the thing that does not save it.

questions.explanation: The route's whole responsibility is the mapping: this address means this screen with these parameters, and when the address changes that is what says which screen replaces the current one and which parameters it gets. Everything else is a separate question that happens to be nearby. The data belongs to whatever fetches it, so two screens with different parameters can share one fetching arrangement; remembering the place across a reload is what putting state in the address is for; and whether a reader may see a screen is a decision made on the server, since a route that runs in the browser is not a place where a rule can be enforced.
questions.hint: Ask what the route is given and what it must decide, ignoring everything downstream of that.

questions.explanation: A part is worth splitting when the reasons to change are different, and here they plainly are: the request changes when the endpoint does, the range changes every time a reader picks a date, the formatting changes when the report gains a column, and the buttons change when a new action is offered. Splitting along those lines means a change to one leaves the others alone, and the request can move into a hook and be reused by a second screen without being copied. Splitting by what is drawn only renames the code, and sharing state is an argument about where the values live rather than a reason to keep every job in one function.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to change for each job to change, and whether those are the same thing.
